description: How TV’s ad dollars cratered, then whiplashed back—while Netflix, YouTube, and Amazon fought for the remaining attention in a high-speed market reset.

youtube_description:
🚨 Chaptered chart-race story: when streaming took ad attention—and then changed the economics of TV.

0:00 — The Ad Fall Line (2009–2012)
TV advertising stays high (~$73B → ~$71B) while streaming is mostly “subscriber” not “ad.” Netflix ad activity is near-zero.

1:10 — The YouTube Acceleration (2013–2016)
YouTube ads climb from ~$16.5B to ~$28B. Amazon edges from ~$17B to ~$28B. The old TV engine starts to lose share (down to ~$58B).

2:20 — Cord-Cutting Hits Harder (2017–2019)
TV keeps sliding (~$56B → ~$50B). Meanwhile, YouTube grows (~$33B → ~$44B) and Amazon scales (~$35B → ~$50B). Netflix begins advertising more aggressively (~$8.5B → ~$14B proxy).

3:30 — 2020 Shock & 2021 Repricing
TV ad spend drops sharply to ~$38B (pandemic uncertainty). YouTube rebounds to ~$62B and Amazon jumps to ~$78B—attention moved online and advertisers chased it.

4:30 — The New Baseline (2022–2026)
TV never fully regains the old peak: ~$41B (2022) drifting to ~$33B by 2026. YouTube rises to ~$110B by 2026, Amazon to ~$158B—and Netflix to ~$46B as the streaming ad model matures.

5:40 — Final Question for the Chart Race
If TV ad budgets cap at ~$33B while YouTube + Amazon surge past ~$268B combined, who “wins” the next decade of ad-supported video?

instagram_caption:
🚀 The $73B TV Fall… and the ad dollars that sprinted online.

For years, streaming wasn’t supposed to “kill” TV ads—it was supposed to just siphon viewers. But the real plot twist is what happened to advertising budgets once brands realized eyeballs were migrating faster than measurement. In our timeline, U.S. TV ad spend drifts from about $73B (2009) down to ~$56B by 2017—an early warning that attention was changing lanes. Netflix’s ad footprint is tiny in the early years (near 0 until the mid-2010s), because the business model was mostly subscribers.

Then the internet’s ad engines started compounding.
YouTube ads climb from ~$16.5B (2013) to ~$33B (2017), while Amazon Ads grows from ~$17B (2013) to ~$35B (2017). Meanwhile TV keeps sliding (~$56B → ~$50B by 2019). This is the moment the “ad-supported future” stopped being theoretical.

2020 is where the chart race gets violent. TV ad spend drops to about $38B. In the same period, YouTube rockets to ~$50B and Amazon jumps to ~$62B—because advertisers didn’t just need impressions; they needed performance and targeting. By 2021, YouTube is ~$62B and Amazon is ~$78B, while TV hovers around ~$40B.

The long ending (2022–2026) is the strangest part: TV never returns to the peak. It falls from ~$41B (2022) to about ~$33B by 2026, while YouTube rises to ~$110B and Amazon to ~$158B. Netflix also increases its ad presence—climbing to ~$46B by 2026—as streaming fully locks in as an ad platform, not just a content destination.

Be honest—what do you think happened faster: viewers leaving TV… or advertisers leaving TV? Drop your answer: 👇 Follow for the next chart race.
facebook_caption:
Streaming didn’t just reshape viewing habits—it rewired where advertising money goes. In 2009, U.S. TV advertising sat around $73B. Over the next decade, the market steadily deteriorated: TV declines to about $56B by 2017 and ~$50B by 2019. 

As TV’s share eroded, digital platforms powered the replacement cycle. YouTube’s ad revenue grows from roughly $16.5B (2013) to ~$44B (2019), while Amazon Ads rises from ~$17B (2013) to about ~$50B (2019). Netflix’s advertising presence remains minimal early on, but accelerates as the ad-supported streaming era matures.

The inflection point arrives in 2020: TV advertising falls to about $38B, while YouTube and Amazon surge (YouTube ~$50B; Amazon ~$62B). By 2021, YouTube reaches ~$62B and Amazon ~$78B, while TV remains near ~$40B. The post-pandemic baseline stays lower: by 2026, TV advertising is projected to be about $33B, contrasted with YouTube at ~$110B and Amazon Ads at ~$158B.

Key takeaway: the “collapse” wasn’t instant—it was a years-long reallocation that became irreversible during the 2020 shock.

What would you bet on next: TV’s comeback, or continued ad dominance by platform video?
